finding: XGBoost produced its strongest and most consistent WRMSSE improvement for smooth demand.
quantitative_evidence: Mean WRMSSE decreased from 0.806369 to 0.635986, an improvement of 21.1297%. XGBoost won all 5 folds.
interpretation: The selected lag, rolling, calendar, event, SNAP and price features were consistently useful for the comparatively regular smooth-demand series.
caveat: The result applies to the balanced experimental subset and should not be generalised automatically to every smooth retail series.

finding: XGBoost also performed consistently well for erratic demand.
quantitative_evidence: Mean WRMSSE decreased from 0.949980 to 0.793776, an improvement of 16.4429%. XGBoost won all 5 folds.
interpretation: High non-zero demand variability did not prevent XGBoost from learning useful nonlinear patterns from the available feature set.
caveat: This is descriptive evidence from five folds and does not establish why particular features produced the improvement.

finding: The overall WRMSSE benefit for intermittent demand was very small and temporally unstable.
quantitative_evidence: Mean WRMSSE decreased from 1.215647 to 1.209538, an improvement of 0.5025%. XGBoost won 4 of 5 folds, but Fold 1 deteriorated by 35.8361%.
interpretation: XGBoost was able to reduce bottom-level forecast errors, but these gains did not consistently translate into improvements across the weighted hierarchy.
caveat: The arithmetic mean of fold-specific improvement percentages was -0.9984%, while the improvement calculated from the two mean WRMSSE scores was 0.5025%. Both summaries must be labelled clearly.

finding: XGBoost improved lumpy-demand forecasting overall, but the result was less stable than for smooth and erratic demand.
quantitative_evidence: Mean WRMSSE decreased from 1.258928 to 1.127514, an improvement of 10.4386%. XGBoost won 4 of 5 folds.
interpretation: The model captured useful patterns in lumpy demand, particularly at detailed hierarchy levels, but was not consistently superior in every time period.
caveat: Fold 1 lumpy WRMSSE deteriorated by 14.9296%, showing that the overall mean conceals temporal variation.

finding: XGBoost improvements were generally stronger at detailed hierarchy levels for intermittent and lumpy demand.
quantitative_evidence: For intermittent demand, mean XGBoost WRMSSE was lower at L7 to L12, with the clearest gains at item, item-state and item-store levels. Lumpy demand also showed its largest mean improvements at L9 to L12.
interpretation: The model appears more effective at modelling series-specific patterns than reproducing the aggregate behaviour of sparse demand.
caveat: This is a descriptive hierarchy comparison. Feature ablation and SHAP are still required before discussing which inputs contributed to the pattern.

finding: MAE and RMSE results were more consistently favourable than WRMSSE results.
quantitative_evidence: XGBoost improved MAE and RMSE in all 20 fold-demand-type comparisons, but improved WRMSSE in 18 of 20 comparisons.
interpretation: Bottom-level error reduction does not guarantee improvement under the weighted hierarchical metric.
caveat: WRMSSE remains the primary metric, so MAE and RMSE improvements cannot be used to dismiss the two WRMSSE losses.

finding: The selected number of boosting rounds varied substantially across folds and demand types.
quantitative_evidence: Selected rounds ranged from 150 to 1,250, with a mean of 475 rounds. Intermittent demand had the highest mean selection at 706 rounds.
interpretation: A single globally fixed tree count would not have represented the validation behaviour of every demand type and time period equally well.
caveat: A greater number of rounds does not necessarily mean that a demand type is inherently more complex.
